children: The artificial intelligence boom has survived years of warnings that it will end like the dot-com frenzy or housing bubble. For now, money is still pouring into AI companies, chips and data centers.
That flow of capital may be the most important thing for investors to watch, The Wall Street Journal reported.

The AI buildout faces plenty of potential obstacles, including power shortages, uncertain demand, rising borrowing costs and competition among model developers. But the more immediate threat could come if investors become unwilling to keep financing companies that require enormous amounts of cash before reaching profitability.

Much of the AI ecosystem is financially interconnected. Model developers need billions of dollars to train and operate their systems, while chipmakers, cloud providers and data-center operators are investing heavily in anticipation of continued AI demand. If major AI companies suddenly struggle to raise capital, the effects could spread to suppliers and infrastructure companies whose growth expectations depend on that spending.

History provides some cautionary examples. During the dot-com collapse, investors began focusing on companies’ cash burn and “funding gaps,” meaning the additional capital businesses needed to survive until they could support themselves.

Pets.com became an extreme example. The company could sustain heavy losses as long as investors were willing to provide fresh money. Once technology stocks collapsed and financing dried up, that model quickly became untenable and the company shut down in 2000.

A similar dynamic appeared during the financial crisis. As mortgage losses mounted, financial institutions increasingly needed outside capital to repair their balance sheets. Freddie Mac’s difficulty raising the kind of equity needed to absorb losses became an early indication of how severely financial conditions were deteriorating.
AI financing remains available
There are some signs of caution in today’s AI market. OpenAI has ruled out an IPO this year, nuclear technology company Holtec (
) paused its offering plans and Anthropic
delayed its planned IPO.
So far, however, those developments don’t amount to a broad shutdown in financing. AI companies still appear capable of attracting substantial private capital.
That is particularly important for privately held OpenAI
and Anthropic
because investors have limited visibility into their finances. Both are spending heavily as they build increasingly expensive AI models and infrastructure.
OpenAI’s
ability to continue raising money also matters well beyond the company itself. Nvidia
and SoftBank
are among the major sources of capital supporting the AI developer, while Oracle
is investing heavily in data centers partly in anticipation of enormous future business from OpenAI
That creates a chain of financial dependencies. As long as capital remains readily available, AI developers can keep spending and their suppliers can continue investing to serve them.

The warning sign would be a meaningful change in investors’ willingness to provide fresh money. If a major AI company develops a genuine funding gap, forcing it to cut spending or expansion plans because financing is no longer readily available, investors may have reason to reassess growth assumptions throughout the AI supply chain.
For now, the financing window remains open. The bigger question is what happens when investors start showing less willingness to keep it that way.

title: AI boom’s biggest risk may be the money spigot running dry
